articles.title: Multi-Agent Systems Don't Fail Inside Agents. They Fail in the Handoffs
articles.excerpt: Splitting one big agent into a team of specialists feels like good engineering. A planner breaks the task down, a researcher gathers data, a writer drafts, a reviewer approves. Clean separation of con…
articles.body: Splitting one big agent into a team of specialists feels like good engineering. A planner breaks the task down, a researcher gathers data, a writer drafts, a reviewer approves. Clean separation of concerns. Smaller prompts. Easier to reason about. Then it ships, and something weird happens: every individual agent looks fine in testing, yet the system as a whole produces wrong answers you can't explain. The reason is that multi-agent systems mostly fail in the handoffs between agents , not inside any single one. Unclear roles, lost context, a reviewer that quietly stopped reviewing. None of that shows up when you test agents one at a time.

articles.title: Should you noindex your tag and category pages? Let's argue about it
articles.excerpt: Automated technical SEO checks that catch indexing blocks and deploy regressions — seotto.com Every blog, docs site and content-heavy app ends up with archive pages: /tags/kubernetes/, /category/tutor…
articles.body: Automated technical SEO checks that catch indexing blocks and deploy regressions — seotto.com Every blog, docs site and content-heavy app ends up with archive pages: /tags/kubernetes/ , /category/tutorials/ , /topics/payments/page/3/ . Content management systems create them automatically, often hundreds of them. And there's a long-running argument about what to do with them in search. One camp adds noindex to every tag and category page as a matter of hygiene. The other says those pages are some of the most useful on the site and should be indexed like anything else. Let's argue about it. The case for noindex Most tag pages are thin. A tag used on one or two posts produces a page with a heading and two excerpts. There's nothing on it that isn't better on the posts themselves.

articles.body: Automated technical SEO checks that catch indexing blocks and deploy regressions — seotto.com You submit https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml in Search Console, and the status column says Couldn't fetch . Or, a little later, Sitemap could not be read . You click the URL, it opens fine in your browser, and you're left wondering what Google is seeing that you aren't. First, some reassurance: "Couldn't fetch" right after submitting is sometimes just Search Console's status not having caught up. Google may not have attempted the fetch yet. If the sitemap is new, wait a day before debugging. If it's still there after a day or two, here's how to find the actual cause.

articles.title: Practical Guide to Redis Distributed Locking: Preventing Duplicate Webhook Execution During Timeouts
articles.excerpt: Practical Guide to Redis Distributed Locking: Preventing Duplicate Webhook Execution During Timeouts System Architecture and Mutual Exclusion Design When integrating with external payment providers or…
articles.body: Practical Guide to Redis Distributed Locking: Preventing Duplicate Webhook Execution During Timeouts System Architecture and Mutual Exclusion Design When integrating with external payment providers or third-party services, webhook delivery timeouts often trigger automatic retries. Without proper idempotency and mutual exclusion mechanisms, these retries can lead to duplicate execution of critical business logic—such as double-charging a customer or fulfilling an order twice. To prevent duplicate webhook execution in a distributed environment, we need a mechanism that generates a deterministic, unique identifier for each incoming payload and acquires an atomic, distributed lock.

articles.title: Travel Itinerary Retrieval Architecture: Node.js Document Versioning
articles.excerpt: Short answer: for a travel itinerary planner, choose a retrieval architecture that versions durable documents for citations, checks live travel details for freshness, and combines both paths when the…
articles.body: Short answer: for a travel itinerary planner, choose a retrieval architecture that versions durable documents for citations, checks live travel details for freshness, and combines both paths when the itinerary needs durable and current context. For a travel itinerary planner, “document versioning” is not a database checkbox. It is a retrieval contract. An answer about a museum opening time, a rail restriction, or a hotel policy should carry the source version and freshness promise that the product can actually keep. Start with the retrieval contract Write down the user-visible answer before selecting an endpoint. For each field, define the retrieval unit (a whole policy, a paragraph, or a fare rule), metadata filters such as destination and effective date, and an allowed age.

articles.title: Why I Chose SMS OTP Queue Ownership (Before Beginner 2FA Login Stack Integration)
articles.excerpt: Integration effort starts with deciding who owns the support request when authentication is unfinished. For a B2B SaaS contact form, my design choice is to give the request a durable queue owner befor…
articles.body: Integration effort starts with deciding who owns the support request when authentication is unfinished. For a B2B SaaS contact form, my design choice is to give the request a durable queue owner before adding SMS OTP delivery, suppression, or status polling; the extra state is justified when a customer needs help precisely because login has failed. TL;DR: evaluate a beginner 2FA login stack by the work required to preserve that ownership through retries and recovery, with delivery and verification tracked separately. Consider a production design exercise, not a report of an incident: I am reviewing a contact form where a warehouse customer reports a missing pickup code, the delivery status remains pending, and the customer submits the form again.

But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end.

articles.title: Don't miss Saturn shine close to the moon on Nov. 20
articles.excerpt: The moon shines with Saturn in the constellation Pisces after sunset on Nov. 20
articles.body: The moon shines close to the ringed giant Saturn after sunset on Nov. 20, presenting a spectacular naked-eye display as the stars of the Great Square of Pegasus twinkle nearby. Saturn's steady light will appear a little over 5 degrees from the 82%-lit moon in the southeastern sky after the sun dips below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length. Moonlight will hide fainter stars from view, though you should be able to spot Algenib, Markab, Alpheratz and Scheat arrayed in a diamond formation above the lunar disk, marking out the asterism of the Great Square of Pegasus in the November sky.
